statement: Two [circles](c:circle) $k_1$, $k_2$ meet at distinct points $P$ and $Q$. For a point $Z \ne P, Q$ on $k_1$, the lines $ZP$ and $ZQ$ meet $k_2$ again at $A$ and $B$. Then the length $|AB|$ does not depend on $Z$.

hypotheses.text: The curves $k_1$ and $k_2$ are distinct [circles](c:circle) that meet at two points $P \ne Q$.
The point $Z$ lies on $k_1$ and differs from $P$ and $Q$.
The points $A$ and $B$ are the second intersection points of $k_2$ with the lines $ZP$ and $ZQ$.

conclusion: The chord length $|AB|$ is the same for every position of $Z$ on $k_1$.

proofs.name: Inscribed angles
proofs.slogan: The chord $AB$ of $k_2$ subtends a fixed angle at $P$, so its length is fixed.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with directed angles of lines taken modulo $\pi$ and with $ZP$, $ZQ$ not tangent to $k_2$ (a tangent case uses the tangent as the line in the same count). The lines $ZP$ and $ZQ$ differ because $Z$ is not on the line $PQ$, so $A \ne B$.

roles.why: Each [circle](c:circle) gives a constant inscribed angle on the common chord $PQ$.
A point $Z \ne P, Q$ on $k_1$ makes the two secants well defined.
The secants carry the points $A$ and $B$ whose chord the proof measures.

steps.slogan: Fix the angle between the two secants at $Z$.
steps.detail: Because $Z$ lies on $k_1$, the [inscribed angle](c:inscribed-angle) theorem gives $\angle(ZP, ZQ) = \gamma_1$. The value $\gamma_1$ depends only on $k_1$ and the chord $PQ$, not on $Z$.

steps.slogan: Fix the angle at $B$ between the common chord and the secant.
steps.detail: On $k_2$ the inscribed angle $\angle(BP, BQ) = \gamma_2$ is constant by the same theorem. The line $BQ$ is the line $ZQ$, so $\angle(BP, ZQ) = \gamma_2$ for every $Z$.

steps.slogan: Add the two angles to get the angle at $P$ between $PA$ and $PB$.
steps.detail: The line $PA$ is the line $ZP$. Hence $\angle(PA, PB) = \angle(ZP, ZQ) + \angle(ZQ, BP) = \gamma_1 - \gamma_2$, a value that does not depend on $Z$.

steps.slogan: Convert the fixed inscribed angle into a fixed chord length.
steps.detail: In the [circle](c:circle) $k_2$ of radius $r_2$, a chord that subtends the inscribed angle $\theta$ has length $2 r_2 |\sin\theta|$. So $|AB| = 2 r_2 |\sin(\gamma_1 - \gamma_2)|$ for all $Z$.

concepts.c:circle: The two circles supply the constant angles $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$.
concepts.c:inscribed-angle: Inscribed angles on the fixed chord $PQ$ stay constant as $Z$ moves.

source.note: Directed-angle proof by the inscribed angle theorem. The theorem is due to N. Altshiller Court (Mathesis, 1925).

statement: The Chu construction is a functor from co-subunary [polycategories](c:polycategory) to symmetric polycategories, and it is [right adjoint](c:is-right-adjoint) to the forgetful functor from [star-polycategories](c:star-polycategory). So it preserves limits and [internal categories](c:internal-category). For a co-subunary 2-polycategory $C$, the double Chu construction $\mathrm{Chu}(Q(C))$ of its polycategory of quintets is an internal category in symmetric polycategories.

hypotheses.text: The structure $C$ is a co-subunary 2-[polycategory](c:polycategory).

conclusion: Chu is right adjoint to the forgetful functor, it preserves limits and internal categories, and $\mathrm{Chu}(Q(C))$ is an internal category in symmetric polycategories.

proofs.name: Right adjoint preserves internal categories
proofs.slogan: Chu is a right adjoint, so it preserves limits and hence internal categories, such as the quintets of $C$.
proofs.scope: An outline: the construction of $\mathrm{Chu}(C)$ and its adjunction rest on the cited paper, and the later steps are formal consequences. The same argument covers any internal category in co-subunary polycategories, not only quintets.

roles.why: Co-subunary [polycategories](c:polycategory) are the source on which Chu and its quintet construction are defined.

steps.slogan: Build the star-polycategory $\mathrm{Chu}(C)$ from the co-subunary polycategory $C$.
steps.detail: Shulman defines $\mathrm{Chu}(C)$ for a co-subunary [polycategory](c:polycategory) $C$ and checks the polycategory axioms. The result is a symmetric polycategory with duals, a [star-polycategory](c:star-polycategory), and the recipe is functorial in $C$.

steps.slogan: Show that Chu is [right adjoint](c:is-right-adjoint) to the forgetful functor $U$.
steps.detail: A polycategory map $P \to \mathrm{Chu}(C)$ from a star-polycategory $P$ corresponds naturally to a map $U(P) \to C$ of co-subunary polycategories. This natural bijection is the adjunction $U \dashv \mathrm{Chu}$.

steps.slogan: Deduce that Chu preserves all limits.
steps.detail: A right adjoint preserves every [limit](c:limit-category-theory) that exists in its source. So $\mathrm{Chu}$ preserves products and pullbacks of co-subunary polycategories.

steps.slogan: Transfer internal category structure across the limit-preserving functor.
steps.detail: An [internal category](c:internal-category) consists of objects of objects and arrows, with source, target, identity and composition maps defined on pullbacks and subject to equations. A functor that preserves pullbacks sends these data and equations to data of the same kind.

steps.slogan: Apply this to the quintet polycategory $Q(C)$ of the 2-polycategory $C$.
steps.detail: The quintets $Q(C)$ form an internal category in co-subunary polycategories: horizontal arrows are the arrows of $C$, vertical arrows are the unary co-unary arrows, and 2-cells are the square 2-cells of $C$. Its image $\mathrm{Chu}(Q(C))$ is an internal category in symmetric polycategories, the double Chu construction.

concepts.c:polycategory: Chu and the quintet construction are defined on polycategories.
concepts.c:star-polycategory: Chu of a co-subunary polycategory has duals, so it is a star-polycategory.
concepts.c:is-right-adjoint: Being a right adjoint gives the preservation of limits.
concepts.c:limit-category-theory: Pullbacks and products are the limits that define internal categories.
concepts.c:internal-category: The double Chu construction is an internal category in polycategories.

source.ref: M. Shulman, The 2-Chu-Dialectica construction and the polycategory of multivariable adjunctions, Theory and Applications of Categories 35 (2020), no. 4, 89-136
source.note: The paper defines the Chu construction on polycategories, shows that it is right adjoint to the forgetful functor, and forms the double Chu construction of the quintets.

statement: Let $K$ be a field finitely generated over its prime field, and $X$ a smooth, geometrically connected $K$-scheme of finite type. Let $\mathrm{Ker}(X/K)$ be the kernel of $\pi_1^{\mathrm{ab}}(X) \to \pi_1^{\mathrm{ab}}(\mathrm{Spec}\,K)$ on [étale fundamental groups](c:etale-fundamental-group). The kernel is finite if $\mathrm{char}\,K = 0$, and its prime-to-$p$ part is finite if $\mathrm{char}\,K = p > 0$.

hypotheses.text: The field $K$ is finitely generated over its prime field.
The scheme $X$ is smooth, geometrically connected and of finite type over $K$.

conclusion: $\mathrm{Ker}(X/K)$ is finite in characteristic $0$, and its prime-to-$p$ part is finite in characteristic $p > 0$.

proofs.name: Galois coinvariants of the Tate module
proofs.slogan: The kernel is a quotient of Galois coinvariants of the geometric abelian fundamental group, and these are finite by torsion bounds.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the Bertini step and the case of characteristic $p$ are in the paper. Dimensions $0$ and $1$ need no reduction to a curve.

roles.why: Geometric connectedness gives the exact sequence of fundamental groups, and smoothness allows the curve reduction.
Finite generation of $K$ gives finitely many roots of unity and finite cyclotomic torsion.

steps.slogan: Express the kernel as an image of Galois coinvariants.
steps.detail: Geometric connectedness gives an exact sequence $\pi_1(X_{\bar K}) \to \pi_1(X) \to \mathrm{Gal}(\bar K/K) \to 1$. After abelianizing, $\mathrm{Ker}(X/K)$ is the image of the coinvariants $\pi_1^{\mathrm{ab}}(X_{\bar K})_{G_K}$, so finiteness of the coinvariants suffices.

steps.slogan: Reduce to a smooth curve by a Bertini and Lefschetz argument.
steps.detail: A Bertini-type theorem gives a smooth, geometrically connected curve $C \subset X$ over $K$. A Lefschetz theorem makes $\pi_1^{\mathrm{ab}}(C_{\bar K}) \to \pi_1^{\mathrm{ab}}(X_{\bar K})$ onto (prime to $p$), and coinvariants of a quotient are a quotient of coinvariants.

steps.slogan: Describe the geometric abelian fundamental group of the curve by its generalized Jacobian.
steps.detail: Let $\bar C$ be the smooth completion of $C$ with $s$ punctures, and $J$ its Jacobian, the [Albanese variety](c:albanese-variety) of $\bar C$. The prime-to-$p$ part of $\pi_1^{\mathrm{ab}}(C_{\bar K})$ is an extension of the Tate module $T(J)$ of the [abelian variety](c:abelian-variety) $J$ by $\hat{\mathbb Z}'(1)^{s-1}$.

steps.slogan: Bound the coinvariants of the torus part and of the Tate module.
steps.detail: The coinvariants of $\hat{\mathbb Z}'(1)$ under $G_K$ are finite, since $K$ has finitely many roots of unity. The dual of $T(J)_{G_K}$ is the group of torsion points $x$ of the dual abelian variety with $\sigma x = \chi(\sigma) x$, where $\chi$ is the cyclotomic character; such $x$ lie over the cyclotomic extension of $K$.

steps.slogan: Show that the torsion over the cyclotomic extension is finite.
steps.detail: Ribet's appendix shows that an abelian variety over a number field has finite torsion over its cyclotomic extension. Over a finite field, Weil's bounds on Frobenius eigenvalues exclude the eigenvalue $q$. The paper extends both to finitely generated $K$, so $T(J)_{G_K}$ is finite, and right exactness of coinvariants finishes the proof.

concepts.c:etale-fundamental-group: The kernel is defined from the abelian étale fundamental groups of $X$ and $\mathrm{Spec}\,K$.
concepts.c:albanese-variety: For a curve the Albanese variety is the Jacobian that carries the Tate module.
concepts.c:abelian-variety: Finiteness of its torsion over the cyclotomic extension bounds the coinvariants.

source.ref: N. M. Katz and S. Lang, Finiteness theorems in geometric classfield theory, with an appendix by K. A. Ribet, L'Enseignement Mathematique (2) 27 (1981), 285-319
source.note: Katz and Lang prove the finiteness; Ribet's appendix, Torsion points of abelian varieties in cyclotomic extensions, supplies the torsion bound.

statement: Let $X$ be a finite group and $T$ a 2-subgroup of $X$. Then $L_{2'}(C_X(T)) \le L_{2'}(X)$, where $L_{2'}(Y)$ is the 2-[layer](c:layer-of-a-group) of $Y$: the product of the minimal subnormal subgroups of $Y$ that map onto components of $Y/O(Y)$.

hypotheses.text: The group $X$ is finite.
The subgroup $T$ is a 2-subgroup of $X$.

proofs.name: Minimal counterexample and generation
proofs.slogan: A minimal counterexample is analyzed with the generation arguments of Gorenstein and Walter, which place every 2-component of the centralizer in the 2-layer.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof of the whole theorem for every finite $X$ and every 2-subgroup $T$. The proof does not use the classification of finite simple groups.

roles.why: Finiteness allows a counterexample of least order.
The 2-group $T$ acts coprimely on $O(X)$ and acts on the 2-components of its centralizer.

steps.slogan: Pass to the quotient of $X$ by its largest normal subgroup of odd order.
steps.detail: The 2-layer is defined modulo $O(X)$. Since $T$ has order prime to $|O(X)|$, coprime action gives $C_{X/O(X)}(T) = C_X(T)\,O(X)/O(X)$. So the inclusion for $X/O(X)$ gives the inclusion for $X$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the inclusion to a statement about each 2-component of the centralizer.
steps.detail: The [layer](c:layer-of-a-group) $L_{2'}(C_X(T))$ is the product of the 2-components $K$ of $C_X(T)$. So the theorem holds exactly when every such $K$ lies in $L_{2'}(X)$.

steps.slogan: Take a counterexample of least order and restrict its structure.
steps.detail: In a minimal counterexample the theorem holds for every proper subgroup of $X$ that contains $T$. This confines a failing 2-component $K$ and the way that $T$ acts on it.

steps.slogan: Force the failing 2-component into the 2-layer by the generation arguments.
steps.detail: The second half of the paper, on generation, shows that such a $K$ must lie in $L_{2'}(X)$. This contradicts the choice of $X$, so no counterexample exists.

concepts.c:layer-of-a-group: The theorem compares the layer of the centralizer with the layer of $X$.

source.ref: D. Gorenstein and J. H. Walter, Balance and generation in finite groups, Journal of Algebra 33 (1975), 224-287
source.note: The paper proves the L-balance theorem together with its generation results.

statement: Let $G$ be finite and $p$ a prime such that every $p$-local subgroup of $G$ is $p$-constrained. Let $A$ be a normal abelian subgroup of a [Sylow](c:sylow-subgroup) $p$-subgroup $S$ with $C_S(A) = A$ and rank at least 3. For each prime $q \ne p$, $C_G(A)$ is transitive on the maximal $A$-invariant $q$-subgroups of $G$.

hypotheses.text: Every $p$-local subgroup of $G$ is $p$-constrained.
The subgroup $A$ is normal and abelian in a [Sylow](c:sylow-subgroup) $p$-subgroup $S$, and $C_S(A) = A$.
The subgroup $A$ has rank at least 3.

conclusion: For every prime $q \ne p$, the group $C_G(A)$ acts transitively on the maximal $A$-invariant $q$-subgroups of $G$.

proofs.name: Local conjugation along corank-one subgroups
proofs.slogan: Generate invariant $q$-subgroups by centralizers of subgroups of $A$, conjugate inside $p$-local subgroups, and join the local conjugations.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof, for all primes $q \ne p$ at once. The proof is the local analysis that Feit and Thompson used inside the odd order theorem.

roles.why: Rank at least 3 makes every corank-one subgroup $B$ of $A$ nontrivial and lets the local pieces overlap.
$p$-constraint gives the local structure that makes maximal invariant $q$-subgroups conjugate.
Normality of $A$ in the [Sylow](c:sylow-subgroup) subgroup $S$ and $C_S(A) = A$ place $A$ inside every local subgroup used.

steps.slogan: Write each invariant $q$-subgroup as generated by centralizers of corank-one subgroups of $A$.
steps.detail: A noncyclic abelian $p$-group $A$ acting on a $q$-group $Q$ with $q \ne p$ gives $Q = \langle C_Q(B) : B \le A,\ A/B \text{ cyclic}\rangle$. Since $A$ has rank at least 3, each such $B$ is nontrivial and has rank at least 2.

steps.slogan: Place each centralizer inside a $p$-local subgroup that contains $A$.
steps.detail: For $1 \ne B \le A$, the group $N_G(B)$ is a $p$-local subgroup that contains $A$, and $C_G(B)$ is normal in it. By hypothesis $N_G(B)$ is $p$-constrained, which controls its $A$-invariant $q$-subgroups.

steps.slogan: Conjugate maximal invariant $q$-subgroups by elements of $C_G(A)$ inside each local subgroup.
steps.detail: Inside each such local subgroup, $p$-constraint and the position of $A$ in $S$ let one conjugate two maximal $A$-invariant $q$-subgroups by an element of $C_G(A)$. This is the local form of the transitivity.

steps.slogan: Join the local conjugations along a chain of subgroups of $A$.
steps.detail: Because $A$ has rank at least 3, the subgroups $B$ overlap, so any two maximal $A$-invariant $q$-subgroups are linked by a chain of local conjugations. The product of their conjugating elements lies in $C_G(A)$ and moves one subgroup to the other.

concepts.c:sylow-subgroup: $A$ sits inside a Sylow $p$-subgroup, which fixes the local subgroups used.

source.ref: W. Feit and J. G. Thompson, Solvability of groups of odd order, Pacific Journal of Mathematics 13 (1963), 775-1029
source.note: The transitivity theorem originates in this paper, where it is used to prove the uniqueness theorem.

statement: Let $G$ be a connected [semisimple Lie group](c:semisimple-lie-group) with finite center and maximal compact subgroup $K$, $W$ its [Weyl group](c:weyl-group), $0 < p \le 2$ and $\varepsilon = 2/p - 1$. The spherical transform maps the $K$-biinvariant $L^p$ Schwartz space onto the $W$-invariant, rapidly decreasing functions holomorphic on the tube of width $\varepsilon\rho$ over the dual of a Cartan subspace.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is a connected [semisimple Lie group](c:semisimple-lie-group) with finite center, and $K$ is a maximal compact subgroup.
The exponent $p$ satisfies $0 < p \le 2$.

conclusion: The spherical transform is a bijection from the $K$-biinvariant $L^p$ Schwartz space $\mathcal C^p(G/\!/K)$ onto the space $\mathcal Z(F_\varepsilon)^W$ of $W$-invariant functions that are holomorphic inside the tube $F_\varepsilon$, smooth up to its boundary and rapidly decreasing.

proofs.name: Abel transform and inversion
proofs.slogan: Transform by the Abel transform and Fourier analysis, estimate the spherical functions on the tube, and invert by the Harish-Chandra formula.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof for all $0 < p \le 2$; the case $p = 2$ is Harish-Chandra's. Anker gave a simpler proof in the Journal of Functional Analysis 96 (1991).

roles.why: The structure theory of $G$ supplies the Abel transform, the Weyl group action and the spherical functions.
The exponent $p$ fixes the width $\varepsilon\rho$ of the tube and the decay of the functions.

steps.slogan: Write the spherical transform as the Fourier transform of the Abel transform.
steps.detail: For a $K$-biinvariant $f$, the Abel transform is $F_f(a) = e^{\rho(\log a)}\int_N f(an)\,dn$ on $A$. Harish-Chandra shows that the spherical transform $\hat f(\lambda)$ equals the Euclidean [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) of $F_f$ at $\lambda$.

steps.slogan: Bound the spherical functions on the tube and the functions of the Schwartz space.
steps.detail: Harish-Chandra's estimates bound $|\varphi_\lambda|$ for $\mathrm{Im}\,\lambda$ in the convex hull of $\varepsilon\,W\rho$. They also bound a function of $\mathcal C^p(G/\!/K)$ by $\varphi_0^{2/p}$ times a rapidly decreasing factor.

steps.slogan: Show that the transform of a Schwartz function lies in the target space.
steps.detail: Integrating the bounds against $f$ shows that $\hat f$ converges and is holomorphic on the open tube and continuous to its boundary. Harish-Chandra's invariant differential operators give rapid decrease. $W$-invariance holds because $\varphi_{w\lambda} = \varphi_\lambda$.

steps.slogan: Recover $f$ from $\hat f$ by the inversion formula to get injectivity.
steps.detail: Harish-Chandra's inversion formula $f(x) = c\int \hat f(\lambda)\,\varphi_\lambda(x)\,|c(\lambda)|^{-2}\,d\lambda$ holds on $\mathcal C^p(G/\!/K) \subseteq \mathcal C^2(G/\!/K)$. So $\hat f = 0$ forces $f = 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that every function of the target space is a spherical transform.
steps.detail: For $h$ in the target space, define $f$ by the inversion integral. Trombi and Varadarajan shift the contour into the tube, estimate $f$ and its derivatives with the bounds on $\varphi_\lambda$, and show that $f \in \mathcal C^p(G/\!/K)$ with $\hat f = h$.

steps.slogan: Combine the three parts into a bijection onto the tube space.
steps.detail: The transform maps into $\mathcal Z(F_\varepsilon)^W$, is injective by inversion, and is onto by the contour shift. So it is a bijection, which is continuous with continuous inverse for the natural topologies.

concepts.c:semisimple-lie-group: The Abel transform and spherical functions come from the structure of $G$.
concepts.c:weyl-group: Its action explains why the transforms are invariant under the Weyl group.
concepts.c:fourier-transform: The spherical transform becomes a Euclidean Fourier transform on the Cartan subspace.

source.ref: P. C. Trombi and V. S. Varadarajan, Spherical transforms on semisimple Lie groups, Annals of Mathematics (2) 94 (1971), 246-303
source.note: The paper proves the isomorphism for $0 < p \le 2$, building on Harish-Chandra's work on the spherical transform.

statement: Let $G$ be a nonabelian finite [simple group](c:simple-group) with a nontrivial abelian [Sylow](c:sylow-subgroup) 2-subgroup. Then $G$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{PSL}_2(q)$ with $q = 2^n \ge 4$ or $q \ge 5$ and $q \equiv 3, 5 \pmod 8$, or to the Janko group $J_1$, or to a Ree group ${}^2G_2(3^{2m+1})$ with $m \ge 1$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is a nonabelian finite [simple group](c:simple-group).
A [Sylow](c:sylow-subgroup) 2-subgroup $S$ of $G$ is abelian and nontrivial.

conclusion: $G$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{PSL}_2(q)$ as above, to $J_1$, or to ${}^2G_2(3^{2m+1})$ with $m \ge 1$.

proofs.name: Fusion, involution centralizers and characterizations
proofs.slogan: Burnside's theorems give nontrivial fusion in $S$, and the analysis of involution centralizers leaves exactly the four families.
proofs.scope: An outline of Walter's proof of completeness. The list overlaps only in $\mathrm{PSL}_2(4) \cong \mathrm{PSL}_2(5)$, and each listed group has an abelian Sylow 2-subgroup by its group order.

roles.why: Simplicity excludes a normal 2-complement and lets the characterization theorems apply.
Abelian $S$ allows Burnside's fusion theorem and fixes the shape of involution centralizers.

steps.slogan: Show that $S$ is not central in its normalizer.
steps.detail: If $N_G(S) = C_G(S)$, Burnside's normal $p$-complement theorem gives a normal 2-complement $H$. Simplicity forces $H = 1$ or $H = G$, which contradicts $G$ nonabelian or $S \ne 1$. So $N_G(S)/C_G(S) \ne 1$, and it controls fusion in $S$.

steps.slogan: Treat $|S| = 4$ by the dihedral case.
steps.detail: A cyclic Sylow 2-subgroup gives a normal 2-complement, so $|S| = 4$ means $S \cong C_2^2$, dihedral of order 4. The Gorenstein–Walter theorem on dihedral Sylow 2-subgroups gives $G \cong \mathrm{PSL}_2(q)$ with $q \equiv 3, 5 \pmod 8$, because $A_7$ has a Sylow subgroup of order 8.

steps.slogan: For $|S| > 4$, show that $S$ is elementary abelian and classify the involution centralizers.
steps.detail: Walter's analysis uses character theory and local group theory. For an involution $t$, it leaves two types: $C_G(t) = S$ with a strongly embedded subgroup, or $C_G(t) = \langle t\rangle \times \mathrm{PSL}_2(r)$ for a field order $r$.

steps.slogan: Identify $G$ by the known characterization of each type.
steps.detail: A group with a strongly embedded subgroup and abelian Sylow 2-subgroup is $\mathrm{PSL}_2(2^n)$ by Bender's theorem. Involution centralizer $2 \times \mathrm{PSL}_2(4)$ gives $J_1$ by Janko, and $2 \times \mathrm{PSL}_2(3^{2m+1})$ gives a Ree group by Ward.

concepts.c:sylow-subgroup: The abelian Sylow 2-subgroup $S$ is the object that the proof studies.

source.ref: J. H. Walter, The characterization of finite groups with abelian Sylow 2-subgroups, Annals of Mathematics (2) 89 (1969), 405-514
source.note: Walter's paper proves the theorem; the characterizations of $J_1$ and of the Ree groups are due to Janko and to Ward.

statement: Let $p$ be an odd prime and $G$ a finite group that is $p$-constrained and [$p$-stable](c:p-stable-group) and has a nontrivial normal $p$-subgroup. For every [Sylow](c:sylow-subgroup) $p$-subgroup $S$, the subgroup $O_{p'}(G)\,Z(J(S))$ is normal in $G$, where $J(S)$ is the [Thompson subgroup](c:thompson-subgroup) of $S$.

hypotheses.text: The prime $p$ is odd.
The group $G$ is $p$-constrained.
The group $G$ is [$p$-stable](c:p-stable-group).
The group $G$ has a nontrivial normal $p$-subgroup.

conclusion: $O_{p'}(G)\,Z(J(S))$ is a normal subgroup of $G$ for every Sylow $p$-subgroup $S$.

proofs.name: Replacement theorem and p-stability
proofs.slogan: Reduce to $O_{p'}(G) = 1$, then combine Glauberman's replacement theorem with $p$-stability to show that $G$ normalizes $Z(J(S))$.
proofs.scope: An outline of Glauberman's proof for every odd $p$. The heart of the proof, the control of $Z(J(S))$, is in the cited paper.

roles.why: Glauberman's replacement theorem needs an odd prime.
$p$-constraint gives $C_G(P) \le P$ for the largest normal $p$-subgroup $P$.
[$p$-stability](c:p-stable-group) puts quadratic elements into $P$.
A nontrivial normal $p$-subgroup makes $P \ne 1$, so the local analysis has content.

steps.slogan: Pass to the quotient by $O_{p'}(G)$ to assume that $O_{p'}(G) = 1$.
steps.detail: The hypotheses pass to $G/O_{p'}(G)$, where $S$ maps isomorphically and $Z(J(S))$ maps onto $Z(J(\bar S))$. Normality of $Z(J(\bar S))$ in the quotient is normality of $O_{p'}(G)Z(J(S))$ in $G$.

steps.slogan: Record the two local consequences of $p$-constraint and $p$-stability.
steps.detail: Let $P = O_p(G)$. With $O_{p'}(G) = 1$, $p$-constraint gives $C_G(P) \le P$. [$p$-stability](c:p-stable-group) gives that every $x \in G$ with $[P, x, x] = 1$ lies in $P$.

steps.slogan: Trade maximal abelian subgroups of $S$ for ones that act quadratically.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal A(S)$ be the abelian subgroups of $S$ of largest order. Glauberman's replacement theorem, for odd $p$, gives from $A \in \mathcal A(S)$ not normalized by a suitable normal subgroup an $A^* \in \mathcal A(S)$ that normalizes $A$ and meets that subgroup in more. Then $[A^*, A, A] = 1$.

steps.slogan: Combine replacement and $p$-stability to control $Z(J(S))$.
steps.detail: Glauberman feeds the quadratic action given by replacement into $p$-stability, whose conclusion places the acting elements in $P$. This yields that $G$ normalizes $Z(J(S))$.

steps.slogan: Lift the normality back to the original group $G$.
steps.detail: Since $Z(J(\bar S))$ is normal in $G/O_{p'}(G)$, its preimage $O_{p'}(G)Z(J(S))$ is normal in $G$.

concepts.c:p-stable-group: $p$-stability forces elements with quadratic action into the largest normal $p$-subgroup.
concepts.c:sylow-subgroup: The Thompson subgroup is taken inside the Sylow subgroup $S$.
concepts.c:thompson-subgroup: The center of $J(S)$ is the characteristic subgroup that the theorem shows is normal.

source.ref: G. Glauberman, A characteristic subgroup of a p-stable group, Canadian Journal of Mathematics 20 (1968), 1101-1135
source.note: The paper proves the ZJ theorem and the replacement theorem that it needs.

statement: Let $M_1, \dots, M_n$ lie in this order on a line $\ell$, and let $C$ be a point off $\ell$. If the [incircles](c:incircle) of the [triangles](c:triangle) $M_iCM_{i+1}$ all have the same radius, then for each $k$ the incircles of the triangles $M_iCM_{i+k}$ have the same radius.

hypotheses.text: The distinct points $M_1, \dots, M_n$ lie in this order on a line $\ell$, and $C$ is not on $\ell$.
The [incircles](c:incircle) of the triangles $M_iCM_{i+1}$ for $1 \le i < n$ have equal radii.

conclusion: For each $k$ with $1 \le k < n$, the triangles $M_iCM_{i+k}$ with $1 \le i \le n - k$ have incircles of equal radius.

proofs.name: Half-angle tangents
proofs.slogan: A tangent half-angle formula turns equal radii into a geometric progression, and powers of its ratio give the radii of the longer triangles.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with $h$ the common distance from $C$ to $\ell$. Positions on $\ell$ are measured from the foot of the perpendicular from $C$.

roles.why: All triangles share the height $h$, and the ordered points give base angles in terms of one parameter.
Equal [incircle](c:incircle) radii make the consecutive ratios of the parameters equal.

steps.slogan: Show that $1 - 2r/h = \tan(\alpha/2)\tan(\beta/2)$ in every [triangle](c:triangle).
steps.detail: Let a triangle have base $c$, base angles $\alpha, \beta$, altitude $h$, inradius $r$ and semiperimeter $s$. Then $\tan(\alpha/2) = r/(s-a)$ and $\tan(\beta/2) = r/(s-b)$, and Heron's formula gives $r^2 = (s-a)(s-b)(s-c)/s$. Also $rs = ch/2$, so $1 - 2r/h = (s-c)/s = \tan(\alpha/2)\tan(\beta/2)$.

steps.slogan: Parametrize the points by tangent half-angles of the rays from $C$.
steps.detail: Put $M_i$ at signed distance $h\tan\varphi_i$ from the foot of the perpendicular, with $\varphi_i$ increasing. In the triangle $M_iCM_j$ with $i < j$ the base angles are $\pi/2 + \varphi_i$ and $\pi/2 - \varphi_j$. With $T_i = \tan(\pi/4 + \varphi_i/2)$, the lemma gives $1 - 2r/h = T_i/T_j$.

steps.slogan: Turn the equal consecutive radii into one constant ratio.
steps.detail: Let $r$ be the common radius of the [incircles](c:incircle) of $M_iCM_{i+1}$ and put $\rho = 1 - 2r/h$. Then $T_i/T_{i+1} = \rho$ for every $i$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the numbers $T_i$ form a geometric progression.
steps.detail: From $T_{i+1} = T_i/\rho$ we get $T_{i+k} = \rho^{-k} T_i$ for all $i$ and $k$ with $i + k \le n$.

steps.slogan: Compute the inradius of $M_iCM_{i+k}$ and see that it does not depend on $i$.
steps.detail: The lemma gives $1 - 2r_{i,k}/h = T_i/T_{i+k} = \rho^k$. So $r_{i,k} = h(1 - \rho^k)/2$, the same for every $i$.

concepts.c:incircle: The theorem compares the radii of incircles of triangles with a common apex.
concepts.c:triangle: Each triangle $M_iCM_j$ has base on $\ell$ and apex $C$.

source.note: Uses the half-angle lemma of Angela Drei's proof; the derivation of the lemma and the progression is written out here.

statement: Five [circles](c:circle) $k_1, \dots, k_5$ have their centers $O_j$ on a circle $\Gamma$, and $k_j$ meets $k_{j+1}$ (indices mod 5) in a point $P_j \in \Gamma$ and a second point $Q_j$. The points $O_1, P_1, O_2, P_2, \dots, O_5, P_5$ occur in this order on $\Gamma$. Then the lines $Q_{j-1}Q_j$ and $Q_{j+1}Q_{j+2}$ meet on $k_{j+1}$.

hypotheses.text: The centers $O_1, \dots, O_5$ of the [circles](c:circle) $k_1, \dots, k_5$ lie on a circle $\Gamma$.
Each $k_j$ meets $k_{j+1}$ (indices mod 5) in a point $P_j \in \Gamma$ and a second point $Q_j$.
The points $O_1, P_1, O_2, P_2, \dots, O_5, P_5$ occur in this cyclic order on $\Gamma$.
The points $Q_j$ are in general position: consecutive ones differ and the two lines used in the conclusion meet in one point.

conclusion: For each $j$, the lines $Q_{j-1}Q_j$ and $Q_{j+1}Q_{j+2}$ meet at a point of $k_{j+1}$, so the five points of the pentagram lie on the circles.

proofs.name: Complex coordinates and directed angles
proofs.slogan: Put $\Gamma$ in the complex plane, compute the directions of the relevant lines, and compare two directed angles to get a concyclic quadruple.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for convex position of the ten points on $\Gamma$, with indices mod 5. The statement is a special case of Miquel's pentagram theorem.

roles.why: Centers on $\Gamma$, the unit circle, make each center a product $u_{j-1}u_j$ of unit numbers.
The points $P_j$ on $\Gamma$ and the reflection definition of $Q_j$ give explicit formulas.
The cyclic order makes each center the midpoint of the arc $P_{j-1}P_j$ for one consistent choice of square roots.
General position makes the lines and the angles in the last two steps well defined.

steps.slogan: Place $\Gamma$ as the unit circle and write every center and chain point through square roots.
steps.detail: Let $P_j = e^{i\theta_j}$ with $\theta_j$ increasing and $\theta_{j+5} = \theta_j + 2\pi$, and let $u_j = e^{i\theta_j/2}$, so $u_{j+5} = -u_j$. The center $O_j$ lies on $\Gamma$ and is equidistant from $P_{j-1}$ and $P_j$, so by the order it is the arc midpoint $u_{j-1}u_j$. Here $P_j = u_j^2$.

steps.slogan: Compute the second intersection points by reflecting $P_j$ in the line of centers.
steps.detail: The line $O_jO_{j+1}$ is the perpendicular bisector of the common chord, so $Q_j$ is the reflection of $P_j$ in it. For unit numbers $a, b$ the reflection of $z$ in the line $ab$ is $a + b - ab\bar z$. Hence $Q_j = u_{j-1}u_j + u_ju_{j+1} - u_{j-1}u_{j+1}$.

steps.slogan: Compute the direction of each pentagon side and of the chords from $P_j$.
steps.detail: For a segment $w$ let $\delta(w) = w/\bar w$, which is $e^{2i\arg w}$. For unit $u, v$: $\delta(u - v) = -uv$ and $\delta(u + v) = uv$. Factoring gives $Q_j - Q_{j-1} = (u_j - u_{j-1})(u_{j+1} + u_{j-2})$, $Q_j - P_j = -(u_j - u_{j-1})(u_j - u_{j+1})$ and $Q_{j+1} - P_j = (u_{j+1} - u_j)(u_j + u_{j+2})$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two directed angles by dividing the direction numbers.
steps.detail: With $u_{j+3} = -u_{j-2}$, the sides give $\delta(Q_{j+1}Q_{j+2})/\delta(Q_{j-1}Q_j) = -u_{j+2}/u_{j-1}$. The chords give $\delta(P_jQ_{j+1})/\delta(P_jQ_j) = -u_{j+2}/u_{j-1}$. So the two directed angles are equal modulo $\pi$.

steps.slogan: Deduce that the meeting point lies on the circle through $P_j$, $Q_j$ and $Q_{j+1}$.
steps.detail: Let $T$ be the meeting point of the lines $Q_{j-1}Q_j$ and $Q_{j+1}Q_{j+2}$. Then $\angle(TQ_j, TQ_{j+1}) = \angle(P_jQ_j, P_jQ_{j+1})$, so $T, P_j, Q_j, Q_{j+1}$ are [concyclic](c:concyclic-points). The circle through $P_j, Q_j, Q_{j+1}$ is $k_{j+1}$, so $T \in k_{j+1}$.

concepts.c:circle: The circles $k_j$ and $\Gamma$ are the objects whose centers and points are computed.
concepts.c:concyclic-points: Four points on one circle give equal directed angles, and conversely.

source.note: Own complex-number proof, checked numerically. The theorem is due to Auguste Miquel, as the five circles case of his pentagram theorem.

statement: Let $T$ be an [algebraic theory](c:algebraic-theory): a category $\mathbb T$ with finite limits whose models in $\mathcal C$ are finite-limit-preserving functors $\mathbb T \to \mathcal C$. The total-space functor $\Sigma$ from indexed sets $(B, (E_b)_b)$ to the [arrow category](c:arrow-category) of $\mathbf{Set}$ induces an equivalence between models of $T$ in the two categories.

hypotheses.text: The [algebraic theory](c:algebraic-theory) $T$ is a category $\mathbb T$ with finite limits, and its models in $\mathcal C$ are finite-limit-preserving functors $\mathbb T \to \mathcal C$.

conclusion: Composition with $\Sigma$ is an [equivalence of categories](c:equivalence-of-categories) from models of $T$ in indexed sets to models of $T$ in the arrow category of $\mathbf{Set}$.

proofs.name: Postcomposition with an equivalence
proofs.slogan: Indexed sets and functions form equivalent categories, and an equivalence induces an equivalence on models of any finite-limit theory.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for any theory $T$ of this kind, including the theory of categories. The last step reads the models as displayed models.

roles.why: Models are finite-limit-preserving functors, so an equivalence of target categories acts on them.

steps.slogan: Define the total-space and fiber functors between indexed sets and functions.
steps.detail: Let $\mathrm{Fam}$ have objects $(B, (E_b)_{b \in B})$ and morphisms $(f, (g_b))$ with $g_b : E_b \to E'_{f(b)}$. Let $\Sigma(B, E) = (\coprod_b E_b \to B)$. Let $\mathrm{Fib}$ send $p : E \to B$ to $(B, (p^{-1}(b))_b)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the two functors form an [equivalence of categories](c:equivalence-of-categories).
steps.detail: The fiber of $\coprod_b E_b \to B$ over $b$ is $E_b$, and the total space of the fibers of $p$ is isomorphic to $E$ over $B$. Both isomorphisms are natural, so $\Sigma$ and $\mathrm{Fib}$ are quasi-inverse equivalences.

steps.slogan: Note that an equivalence preserves finite limits, so $\Sigma$ carries models to models.
steps.detail: An equivalence of categories preserves all limits that exist. So for a finite-limit-preserving $M : \mathbb T \to \mathrm{Fam}$, the composite $\Sigma \circ M$ preserves finite limits and is a model in the arrow category.

steps.slogan: Show that postcomposition with $\Sigma$ is an equivalence of the categories of models.
steps.detail: Postcomposition with $\mathrm{Fib}$ is the inverse in the same way. The natural isomorphisms $\mathrm{Fib}\,\Sigma \cong \mathrm{id}$ and $\Sigma\,\mathrm{Fib} \cong \mathrm{id}$ give natural isomorphisms of the composites. Homomorphisms of models are natural transformations and correspond one to one.

steps.slogan: Read the two sides as displayed models and homomorphisms of models.
steps.detail: A model in $\mathrm{Fam}$ is a model $B$ of $T$ in $\mathbf{Set}$ with a displayed model over it. A model in the arrow category is a homomorphism of models $E \to B$ in $\mathbf{Set}$. For the theory of categories this is the passage from a [displayed category](c:displayed-category) over $B$ to a functor into $B$.

concepts.c:algebraic-theory: The theory $T$ fixes which functors count as models.
concepts.c:arrow-category: Models in the arrow category are homomorphisms of models in $\mathbf{Set}$.
concepts.c:equivalence-of-categories: The equivalence between indexed sets and functions transfers to models.
concepts.c:displayed-category: For the theory of categories, models in indexed sets are displayed categories.

source.note: Formal argument via the equivalence of indexed sets with the arrow category of Set; the statement follows the nLab page T-Grothendieck construction.

statement: Let $G$ be a nonabelian finite [simple group](c:simple-group) of odd order all of whose proper subgroups are solvable, and let $E$ be an elementary abelian $p$-subgroup of order $p^3$. Then exactly one [maximal subgroup](c:maximal-subgroup) of $G$ contains $E$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is a nonabelian finite [simple group](c:simple-group) of odd order, and every proper subgroup of $G$ is solvable.
The subgroup $E$ is elementary abelian of order $p^3$ for a prime $p$.

proofs.name: Local analysis with transitivity
proofs.slogan: Use the local structure of a minimal simple group and the transitivity theorem to show that two maximal subgroups through $E$ coincide.
proofs.scope: An outline of the original local argument, which is a step in the proof of the Feit–Thompson theorem; that theorem makes the statement vacuous. At least one maximal subgroup contains $E$, because $E$ is a proper subgroup.

roles.why: Solvable proper subgroups are $p$-constrained, which the transitivity theorem needs.
Rank 3 supplies abelian subgroups of rank at least 3 for the transitivity theorem.

steps.slogan: Record the local structure of a minimal simple group of odd order.
steps.detail: Every proper subgroup of $G$ is solvable, so every $p$-local subgroup is $p$-constrained by the Hall–Higman lemma. Hence the hypotheses of the transitivity theorem hold in $G$ for the prime $p$.

steps.slogan: Choose a normal abelian subgroup of rank at least 3 in a Sylow subgroup through $E$.
steps.detail: Let $M$ be a maximal subgroup containing $E$. In a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $M$ through $E$, the proof finds a suitable normal abelian subgroup $A$ of rank at least 3. This is where the rank 3 of $E$ enters.

steps.slogan: Apply the transitivity theorem to $A$.
steps.detail: For every prime $q \ne p$, the group $C_G(A)$ acts transitively on the maximal $A$-invariant $q$-subgroups of $G$.

steps.slogan: Compare two maximal subgroups through $E$ and show that they coincide.
steps.detail: Let $M$ and $N$ contain $E$. Their $A$-invariant $q$-subgroups lie in maximal ones that $C_G(A)$ permutes transitively. A Frattini-type argument then gives $N = M$ by maximality.

concepts.c:simple-group: Simplicity makes every maximal subgroup a proper subgroup with strong local structure.
concepts.c:maximal-subgroup: The theorem says that only one maximal subgroup contains $E$.

source.ref: W. Feit and J. G. Thompson, Solvability of groups of odd order, Pacific Journal of Mathematics 13 (1963), 775-1029 (Theorems 24.5 and 25.2)
source.note: Bender gave a shorter proof: H. Bender, On the uniqueness theorem, Illinois Journal of Mathematics 14 (1970), 376-384.

statement: For an integer $n \ge 3$, the number $n$ is [prime](c:prime-number) if and only if $\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}(2^k - 1) \equiv n \pmod{2^n - 1}$.

hypotheses.text: The number $n$ is an integer with $n \ge 3$.

conclusion: The [congruence](c:congruence) $\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}(2^k - 1) \equiv n \pmod{2^n - 1}$ holds exactly when $n$ is prime.

proofs.name: Cyclotomic congruence and largest prime factor
proofs.slogan: For prime $n$ the congruence is the polynomial congruence modulo the cyclotomic polynomial at $X = 2$, and for composite $n$ the largest prime factor gives a contradiction.
proofs.scope: The congruence modulo $2^n - 1$ for all $n \ge 3$. The first polynomial form in the statement of Vantieghem's theorem is the identity of the first step.

roles.why: Oddness of $n \ge 3$ gives the sign $(-1)^{n-1} = 1$, and $n \ge 3$ makes the factor $2^p - 1$ exceed 1.

steps.slogan: Show that $\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}(X^k - 1) \equiv n$ modulo $\Phi_n(X)$ for an odd prime $n$.
steps.detail: Let $\zeta$ be a primitive $n$-th [root of unity](c:root-of-unity). Since $\Phi_n(X) = \prod_{k=1}^{n-1}(X - \zeta^k)$ for prime $n$, we get $\prod_k (\zeta^k - 1) = (-1)^{n-1}\Phi_n(1) = n$. The [cyclotomic polynomial](c:cyclotomic-polynomial) $\Phi_n$ is monic and irreducible by Eisenstein, so it divides $\prod_k (X^k - 1) - n$ in $\mathbb Z[X]$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the polynomial congruence at $X = 2$ to prove the forward direction.
steps.detail: For prime $n$, $\Phi_n(2) = 1 + 2 + \dots + 2^{n-1} = 2^n - 1$. So $2^n - 1$ divides $\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}(2^k - 1) - n$, which is the [congruence](c:congruence).

steps.slogan: For composite $n$ with largest prime factor $p$, reduce the congruence modulo $2^p - 1$.
steps.detail: Assume the congruence for composite $n$. Since $p \mid n$ and $p < n$, we have $(2^p - 1) \mid (2^n - 1)$ and the factor $k = p$ occurs in the product. So the product is $0$ modulo $2^p - 1$, and hence $(2^p - 1) \mid n$.

steps.slogan: Take a prime factor of $2^p - 1$ and contradict the choice of $p$.
steps.detail: Let $q$ be a prime with $q \mid 2^p - 1$. Then $q \mid n$, the order of $2$ modulo $q$ is $p$, and Fermat's little theorem gives $p \mid q - 1$, so $q > p$. This contradicts that $p$ is the largest prime factor of $n$, so the congruence fails.

steps.slogan: Combine both directions into the equivalence.
steps.detail: A prime $n \ge 3$ satisfies the congruence by the forward direction. A composite $n$ does not, by the contradiction. So the congruence holds exactly when $n$ is [prime](c:prime-number).

concepts.c:prime-number: The theorem is a primality criterion.
concepts.c:congruence: The criterion is a congruence modulo $2^n - 1$.
concepts.c:root-of-unity: A primitive root of unity turns the product into the value $\Phi_n(1)$.
concepts.c:cyclotomic-polynomial: Its value at $X = 2$ is the modulus $2^n - 1$.

source.note: Own proof; the polynomial identity is the first polynomial form of Vantieghem's theorem.

statement: Let $G$ be a finite [simple group](c:simple-group) whose [Sylow](c:sylow-subgroup) 2-subgroup is quasidihedral or wreathed ($C_{2^n} \wr C_2$ with $n \ge 2$). Then $G$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{PSL}_3(q)$ or $\mathrm{PSU}_3(q)$ for an odd $q$, the choice depending on $q$ modulo 4, or to the [Mathieu group](c:mathieu-group) $M_{11}$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is a finite [simple group](c:simple-group).
A [Sylow](c:sylow-subgroup) 2-subgroup of $G$ is quasidihedral or wreathed.

conclusion: $G$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{PSL}_3(q)$ or $\mathrm{PSU}_3(q)$ for an odd $q$, or to $M_{11}$.

proofs.name: Block theory and local analysis
proofs.slogan: Brauer's block theory restricts the involution centralizers of a group with such a Sylow 2-subgroup, and the local structure identifies the group.
proofs.scope: An outline of the 261-page paper, which settles the quasidihedral case and a major part of the wreathed case. The remaining wreathed cases were completed by the same authors in a later paper on simple groups of 2-rank two.

roles.why: Simplicity excludes a normal 2-complement and a nontrivial normal subgroup in the local analysis.
The Sylow type fixes the fusion pattern and the defect group of the principal 2-block.

steps.slogan: Fix the Sylow 2-subgroup and the fusion of its involutions.
steps.detail: Let $S$ be quasidihedral or wreathed and $z$ a central involution of $S$. The group $S$ has few classes of involutions, so the fusion of involutions in $G$ is limited to a short list of patterns.

steps.slogan: Apply Brauer's block theory to the principal 2-block with defect group $S$.
steps.detail: The ordinary and modular characters of the principal 2-block, whose defect group is $S$, restrict the values of characters on involutions. This restricts $C_G(z)$ and the fusion patterns.

steps.slogan: Determine the possible centralizers of involutions.
steps.detail: Using these restrictions, the paper finds the structure of $C_G(z)$ and of the other 2-local subgroups. They match those of $\mathrm{PSL}_3(q)$, $\mathrm{PSU}_3(q)$ or $M_{11}$, according to the type of $S$ and the class of $q$ modulo 4.

steps.slogan: Identify $G$ from its local structure.
steps.detail: The local data of the last step characterize the three families. So $G$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{PSL}_3(q)$ or $\mathrm{PSU}_3(q)$ with $q$ odd, or to $M_{11}$.

concepts.c:simple-group: Simplicity restricts the possible normal structure of the local subgroups.
concepts.c:sylow-subgroup: The type of the Sylow 2-subgroup is the hypothesis that drives the analysis.
concepts.c:mathieu-group: $M_{11}$ is the sporadic group that occurs with quasidihedral Sylow subgroups.

source.ref: J. L. Alperin, R. Brauer and D. Gorenstein, Finite groups with quasi-dihedral and wreathed Sylow 2-subgroups, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 151 (1970), 1-261
source.note: The paper classifies the simple groups with quasidihedral Sylow 2-subgroups and gives a major part of the wreathed case.

statement: Let $p$ be a prime with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 8$. If $p \equiv 1 \pmod{16}$, then $p$ is represented by both or by neither of the [quadratic forms](c:quadratic-form) $x^2 + 32y^2$ and $x^2 + 64y^2$. If $p \equiv 9 \pmod{16}$, then $p$ is represented by exactly one of them.

hypotheses.text: The number $p$ is a prime with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 8$.

conclusion: For $p \equiv 1 \pmod{16}$ the two [forms](c:quadratic-form) represent $p$ together or not at all, and for $p \equiv 9 \pmod{16}$ exactly one of them represents $p$.

proofs.name: Indices of 2 and of -4
proofs.slogan: Express both representations as power conditions on $2$ and $-4$, then compare their indices modulo $8$.
proofs.scope: Primes $p \equiv 1 \pmod 8$, which covers $p \equiv 1$ and $p \equiv 9 \pmod{16}$. The proof rests on Gauss's fourth-power criterion for $2$ and the Barrucand–Cohn eighth-power criterion for $-4$.

roles.why: The condition $p \equiv 1 \pmod 8$ makes $2$ a square, so its index $a$ is even and $8 \mid p - 1$.

steps.slogan: Fix a primitive root and the index of $2$.
steps.detail: Let $g$ be a primitive root modulo $p$ and $2 \equiv g^a$. Since $p \equiv 1 \pmod 8$, the number $2$ is a square, so $a$ is even. Also $-1 \equiv g^{(p-1)/2}$.

steps.slogan: Translate $x^2 + 64y^2$ into a fourth-power condition on $2$.
steps.detail: By Gauss, $p = x^2 + 64y^2$ exactly when $2$ is a fourth power modulo $p$. That is the condition $4 \mid a$.

steps.slogan: Translate $x^2 + 32y^2$ into an eighth-power condition on $-4$.
steps.detail: By Barrucand and Cohn, $p = x^2 + 32y^2$ exactly when $-4$ is an eighth power modulo $p$. The index of $-4$ is $(p-1)/2 + 2a$ modulo $p - 1$, so the condition is $8 \mid (p-1)/2 + 2a$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two conditions in each class of $p$ modulo 16.
steps.detail: If $p \equiv 1 \pmod{16}$, then $(p-1)/2 \equiv 0 \pmod 8$, so the eighth-power condition is $4 \mid a$: both forms represent $p$ or neither does. If $p \equiv 9 \pmod{16}$, then $(p-1)/2 \equiv 4 \pmod 8$, so it is $a \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, the opposite of $4 \mid a$ for even $a$: exactly one form does.

concepts.c:quadratic-form: Representation of $p$ by the forms $x^2 + 32y^2$ and $x^2 + 64y^2$ is the subject.

source.note: Kaplansky's argument uses that 2 is a fourth power modulo p exactly when p = x^2 + 64y^2, and that -4 is an eighth power exactly when p = x^2 + 32y^2.
